text: Every system you've secured so far has one property in common: its behavior is fixed by code you can read, so you can validate input against rules you defined. A large language model breaks that assumption in three specific ways, and none of them mean your existing skills stop mattering — API security, access control, and data protection are still just as important. It means there's a new layer on top of them that those disciplines were never built to inspect.

First, natural language becomes a command channel instead of just data, because the model reads instructions and user content as the same kind of material — that's what makes prompt injection possible. Second, output is probabilistic: the same prompt can produce different results on different runs, which breaks deterministic regression testing and lets a rephrased input slip past a keyword filter. Third, training data and model weights become assets you now have to protect — a model can memorize and later leak fragments of what it was trained on, and stolen weights are stolen intellectual property.

SQL injection works because a database engine gets tricked into treating data as code — there's a parsing bug to exploit, and parameterized queries close it. Prompt injection works for a different reason entirely: the model was never given a hard boundary between content it's told to process and instructions it's told to follow in the first place. Text pasted in from an email or a scraped web page can be read as a new command, and there's no prepared statement that fixes a boundary that was never there.

That non-determinism cuts two ways operationally. You can't fully regression-test an LLM feature the way you'd test a deterministic function, because passing once doesn't guarantee passing again. And a fixed keyword blocklist is easy to defeat just by rephrasing, since the attack surface is the space of everything that can be phrased, not a fixed list of bad strings. Meanwhile training data poisoning and weight theft open failure modes that simply didn't exist in traditional application security.

None of this retires the fundamentals — it adds a layer on top of them. Next, you'll see the real, published catalog that names these risks precisely: the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, the industry-standard reference for exactly what this new layer introduces.
